summary: Specifies ways to adjust how often SIP event notifications are sent, such as limiting their rate. The mechanisms work in subscriptions to any SIP event package. It updates RFC 3265.

eli5.summary: If a friend texts you every second, you may ask for fewer. This lets a SIP subscriber ask the sender to slow down the updates it gets.

questions: how to limit sip notification rate
how to pause sip event notifications
subtitle: Three Event header parameters let a SIP subscriber set a ceiling, a floor or an adaptive floor on how often it is notified.

tldr.problem: The SIP events framework only fixes a per-package maximum notification rate, so a subscriber cannot ask for fewer updates, or for guaranteed periodic ones, on its own subscription.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber adds max-rate, min-rate or adaptive-min-rate to the Event header field of a SUBSCRIBE. The notifier may adjust the value and must echo it back in the Subscription-State header field of NOTIFY requests.
tldr.outcome: Subscribers can throttle, pause or force periodic notifications on any event package. The RFC updates RFC 3265 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6446 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, and it updates RFC 3265.

sections.title: Why Notification Rate Needs Control
sections.content:
The SIP events framework (RFC 3265) defines the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods and the idea of an event package. Each package must define an absolute maximum notification rate for a single notifier, to reduce network load. Existing packages recommend anything from one notification every five seconds to one per second. None of them defines a way for the subscriber to limit the rate further.

The resource list extension (RFC 4662) lets a Resource List Server (RLS) buffer notifications and send them in batches, but the subscriber cannot set the interval. Some packages also want a minimum rate, so that the subscriber periodically receives current state even when no trigger criteria fire.

RFC 6446 adds three Event header field parameters: max-rate, min-rate and adaptive-min-rate. They work for any event package, for single subscriptions and for list subscriptions.
sections.eli5: A notifier is like a friend who sends you news. Until now you could not say how often you want to hear from them. Now you can ask for fewer messages, or for at least a few.

sections.title: Use Cases and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC motivates the three parameters with examples. A presence client watching 100 buddies through an RLS sets a maximum rate so the RLS batches changes into one notification. If the user goes idle, the client can pause notifications by choosing a max-rate that allows only a single notification for the rest of the subscription, then resume later by re-subscribing with the earlier value.

A location application using filters that fire only when a target moves some distance may still want fresh state periodically, so it sets a minimum rate. A third application wants the minimum to rise or fall depending on how many notifications were sent recently, which is the adaptive minimum.

The requirements list (REQ1 to REQ10) says the three mechanisms must be usable alone or together, with any event package and with other filters. They must be changeable during an active subscription. The notifier may adjust the values by policy, corner cases such as a gap longer than the subscription must be handled, and authentication and integrity protection must be possible.
sections.eli5: Imagine watching 100 friends online. You do not want a buzz for every tiny change, so you ask for a summary every little while. You can also say pause, or tell them to check in at least now and then.

sections.title: Basic Negotiation
sections.content:
A subscriber requests rate control by putting max-rate, min-rate or adaptive-min-rate in the Event header field of a SUBSCRIBE. To change a value, it sends the updated parameters in a later SUBSCRIBE or in the Event header field of a 2xx response to a NOTIFY. Leaving a parameter out of that request or response removes that control. If the most recent SUBSCRIBE in a dialog had none of the three parameters, the subscriber must not put them in a 2xx response to NOTIFY.

The notifier must adjust its rate to the values agreed. It may raise or lower the requested values, for example because of local policy or because it must shorten the subscription expiration. It must reflect the possibly adjusted values in the same-named parameters of the Subscription-State header field in later NOTIFY requests. A notifier that does not understand the extension simply never echoes them, and that absence tells the subscriber that no rate control is supported.

Each value is a positive real number of notifications per second in a finite decimal form. The grammar limits it to between 0.0000000001 and 99.9999999999, and zero is not allowed. The mechanisms govern new transactions only, so retransmissions of NOTIFY are unaffected.
sections.eli5: You tell the sender your wish when you sign up. The sender replies with the rate it will really use, which might differ a bit. If it says nothing, it does not know the trick.

sections.title: Maximum Rate
sections.content:
With max-rate, a compliant notifier must not generate a notification if the time since the last one is less than the reciprocal of the value. The exceptions are a notification on receipt of a SUBSCRIBE, one when the subscription moves from pending to active, and the final one when the subscription ends. A notifier whose local policy sets a maximum rate keeps to it even if the subscriber asks for none, and may tell the subscriber through max-rate in Subscription-State.

The RFC warns that a maximum rate whose interval exceeds the subscription expiration would quench the notifier, leaving exactly two notifications. In that case the notifier must raise the maximum to the reciprocal of the remaining expiration time, and do the same if it later shortens the expiry. A subscriber that wants to pause the stream should set the rate to the reciprocal of the remaining expiration time.

For a list subscription, the rate applies to the aggregate stream, not to each resource. Notifications that pile up in a buffer are merged by type: for full-state packages only the most recent full state of each resource is kept, and for partial-state packages the deltas are merged. The downsides are that state transitions may be lost and notifications delayed, so developers who cannot accept that are told not to use the mechanism.
sections.eli5: It is like a rule that the mailman may only knock once every so often. Letters that pile up are bundled, and only the newest news about each thing is kept.

sections.title: Minimum and Adaptive Minimum Rate
sections.content:
With min-rate, a compliant notifier must generate a notification when state changes or when the time since the last one exceeds the reciprocal of the value. The body carries the current full state or the partial state, depending on the package and the subscriber's preferences. If both sides support RFC 5839, the request or its body can be suppressed when nothing has changed. The subscriber should request the lowest possible minimum, because a high one creates load and may repeat known state.

The adaptive version lets the gap vary. The notifier keeps a count of notifications sent in the last period seconds, starting as if it had sent period * adaptive-min-rate of them. If the computed timeout passes with no NOTIFY, it sends the current state. After every NOTIFY it updates count and recalculates.

The timeout formula is timeout = count / ((adaptive-min-rate ^ 2) * period). When max-rate is also set, it becomes MAX[(1/max-rate), count/((adaptive-min-rate ^ 2)*period)]. The period must be greater than the reciprocal of adaptive-min-rate, and several times larger is recommended. A notifier may use another algorithm, but it must still comply with any negotiated max-rate or min-rate.
sections.eli5: Minimum rate says: check in with me at least this often, even with no news. The adaptive kind waits longer after a busy spell and checks in sooner after a quiet one.

sections.title: Combining the Mechanisms
sections.content:
The three parameters can be combined and are not technically incompatible, but some combinations make little sense. Maximum plus minimum gives a reduced rate with periodic notifications assured. Maximum plus adaptive minimum does the same with an interval that changes dynamically. Minimum plus adaptive minimum guards against the adaptive mechanism producing a long silence after a burst of changes. Using all three is allowed but described as making little sense.

The ordering rules are simple. A subscriber should choose min-rate and adaptive-min-rate lower than max-rate, otherwise the notifier must lower them to a value equal to or below max-rate. A subscriber should choose min-rate lower than adaptive-min-rate, otherwise the notifier must not consider min-rate.
sections.eli5: You can set a speed limit and a not-too-quiet rule together. Just keep them sensible: the not-too-quiet rule has to be gentler than the speed limit.

sections.title: Protocol Elements, IANA and Security
sections.content:
The new parameters are added to the event-param and subexp-params alternatives in the RFC 3265 grammar. Each is written as the parameter name, an equals sign and one or two digits optionally followed by a dot and up to ten more digits. The Event header field is also now allowed in a 2xx response to NOTIFY. Its event type must match that of the NOTIFY, and other Event parameters in that response must be ignored by the notifier.

IANA registers the three parameters for both the Event and Subscription-State header fields in the SIP parameters registry, and updates the Event header field reference.

For security, everything in RFC 3265 applies, and authentication and message integrity should be used on these subscriptions. Integrity protection should also cover the Event header field in the 2xx response to NOTIFY. Without it, an eavesdropper could modify the field, or manipulate the 200 (OK) response to suppress or flood notifications unnoticed. When partial-state notifications are used with the maximum rate, the considerations of RFC 5263 also apply.
sections.eli5: Anyone who could tamper with your request might make you miss messages or get flooded. So the messages should be protected so nobody can change them on the way.

cells: No new notification if less than 1/max-rate has passed, apart from a few exceptions
Notify on a state change or when more than 1/min-rate has passed
Notify when the computed timeout passes with no NOTIFY sent

data.code:

timeout = MAX[(1/max-rate), count/((adaptive-min-rate ^ 2)*period)] (2)
